findings.title: Pod shares the host network or PID namespace
findings.remediation:
Set hostNetwork and hostPID to false (or omit them; both default to false).
A pod in the host's network namespace can sniff and spoof traffic for every other pod on
the node, and one in the host PID namespace can see and signal every process on the
node, including other tenants' workloads.

findings.title: Container has no resource limits or requests
findings.remediation:
Add a resources block with both limits and requests for cpu and memory.
A container with no ceiling can starve every other workload on the node (or be starved
by one), and the scheduler cannot bin-pack a pod whose requests are unset.

findings.title: Container image pinned to the mutable :latest tag
findings.remediation:
Pin the image to an immutable reference - a specific semver tag the registry
will not overwrite, or better, a content-addressed digest (`@sha256:...`). `:latest`
(or no tag at all, which defaults to it) means the same manifest can deploy a different
image tomorrow with no corresponding change to review, and a rollback cannot pin to
"what was actually running."

findings.title: Container runs with privileged escalation enabled
findings.remediation:
Remove `privileged: true` from the container's securityContext.
A privileged container has near-complete access to the host - device nodes, kernel
capabilities, and namespaces - so almost every real workload can run instead with a
narrow, explicit `capabilities.add` list for only the capability it actually needs.

findings.title: Container has no explicit non-root execution guard
findings.remediation:
Set securityContext.runAsNonRoot to true (and pair it with a non-zero
runAsUser) at the pod or container level. Without it, the container image's own
default user applies, which for most public base images is root - a container
breakout then lands the attacker in the host's root context rather than an
unprivileged one.

findings.title: Pod does not disable automatic service-account token mounting
findings.remediation:
Set automountServiceAccountToken to false on the pod spec (or the
ServiceAccount) unless the workload genuinely calls the Kubernetes API. The default is
true, so every pod otherwise carries a live, mountable credential for its service
account into a container that most workloads never use it from - exactly what a
container-escape or SSRF exploit looks for next.
